e2d92507-9294-550b-bb70-20e6e46f340d.title: Solving a Radially Projected Model for Velocity

e-21748.problem: Consider a spherical  planet with radius $(6.3\times10^6)\,\textrm{m}$ and surface gravitational acceleration $g = 9.7\,\textrm{m/s}^2.$ Which differential equation best models the velocity $v$ of an object projected radially outward from the planet, where $r$ is the distance from the planet's center to the object? Assume the only force acting on the object is the force due to gravity.
e-21748.worked_solution:
According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, the magnitude of the inward gravitational force pulling the object toward the planet is

$$
F_\text{in} = G\,\dfrac{mM}{r^2},
$$

where $G$ is the gravitational constant, $m$ is the object's mass, and $M$ is the planet's mass.

Since this is the only force and it acts inward, the resultant force, taking *outward* as positive, is $F=-F_\textrm{in}.$
Applying Newton's second law, $F=ma,$ where $a$ is the acceleration of the object, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =-{F}_{\text{in}} \\ ma & =-G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}} \\ a & =-\frac{GM}{{r}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the acceleration is inversely proportional to the square of the distance,

$$
a=-\dfrac{k}{r^2},
$$

with constant of proportionality $k=GM > 0.$

When at the surface, $r=(6.3\times10^6)\,\textrm{m},$ the acceleration of the object due to gravity is $a=-9.7\,\textrm{m/s}^2.$ Substituting into our previous equation, we can solve for $k{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}-9.7 & =-\frac{k}{(6.3\times {10}^{6})^{2}} \\ k & =9.7\cdot (6.3\times {10}^{6})^{2} \\  & =9.7\cdot (6.3)^{2}\times ({10}^{6})^{2} \\  & =384.993\times {10}^{12} \\  & =3.84993\times {10}^{14}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting back into the equation, we get

$$
a = -\dfrac{3.84993\times10^{14}}{r^2}.
$$

Finally, since acceleration $a$ is the derivative of velocity $v,$ which is the derivative of distance $r,$ we can express acceleration as follows using the chain rule, treating $v$ as a function of $r$ along the trajectory:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{dv}{dt} \\  & =\frac{dr}{dt}\cdot \frac{dv}{dr} \\  & =v\frac{dv}{dr}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, substituting this result into our equation, we obtain a separable differential equation for the velocity:

$$
v\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}r} = -\dfrac{3.84993\times10^{14}}{r^2}
$$

e-21749.knowledge_point: Solving a Radially Projected Model for Velocity
e-21749.problem: Consider a spherical planet with radius $(8\times10^5)\,\textrm{m}$ and surface gravitational acceleration $g = 16\,\textrm{m/s}^2.$ Which equation best models the velocity $v$ of an object projected radially outward from the planet's surface with an initial velocity of $(9\times10^{4})\,\textrm{m/s},$ where $r$ is the distance from the planet's center to the object. Assume the only force acting on the object is the force due to gravity.
e-21749.worked_solution:
Let $R$ be the planet's radius and $g$ be the planet's surface gravitational acceleration.

According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, the magnitude of the inward gravitational force pulling the object toward the planet is

$$
F_\text{in} = G\,\dfrac{mM}{r^2},
$$

where $G$ is the gravitational constant, $m$ is the object's mass, and $M$ is the planet's mass.

Since this is the only force and it acts inward, the resultant force, taking *outward* as positive, is $F=-F_\textrm{in}.$
Applying Newton's second law, $F=ma,$ where $a$ is the acceleration of the object, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =-{F}_{\text{in}} \\ ma & =-G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}} \\ a & =-\frac{GM}{{r}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the acceleration is inversely proportional to the square of the distance, 

$$
a=-\dfrac{k}{r^2},
$$

 with constant of proportionality $k=GM > 0.$

When at the surface, $r=R,$ the acceleration of the object due to gravity is $a=-g.$ Substituting into our previous equation, we can solve for $k{:}$

$$
-g = -\dfrac{k}{R^2} 
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
k = gR^2
$$

Substituting back into the equation, we get

$$
a = -\dfrac{gR^2}{r^2}.
$$

Now, since acceleration $a$ is the derivative of velocity $v,$ which is the derivative of distance $r,$ we can express acceleration as follows using the chain rule, treating $v$ as a function of $r$ along the trajectory:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{dv}{dt} \\  & =\frac{dr}{dt}\cdot \frac{dv}{dr} \\  & =v\frac{dv}{dr}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this result into our equation, we obtain a separable differential equation for the velocity:

$$
v\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}r} = -\dfrac{gR^2}{r^2}
$$

Solving using separation of variables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int v\frac{dv}{dr}\,dr & =\int (-\frac{g{R}^{2}}{{r}^{2}})\,dr \\ \int v\,dv & =-g{R}^{2}\int \frac{1}{{r}^{2}}\,dr \\ \frac{{v}^{2}}{2} & =-g{R}^{2}(-\frac{1}{r})+{C}_{1} \\ {v}^{2} & =\frac{2g{R}^{2}}{r}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $C=2C_1$ is a constant of integration.

Let $v_0$ be the initial velocity of the object. Applying the initial condition $v(R) = v_0,$ we can solve for $C{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(R)^{2} & =\frac{2g{R}^{2}}{R}+C \\ {v}_{0}^{2} & =2gR+C \\ C & ={v}_{0}^{2}-2gR\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation for the velocity of the object is

$$
v^2 = \dfrac{2gR^2}{r} + v_0^2 - 2gR.
$$

Finally, substituting in the values
$R=(8\times10^5),$
$g=16,$ and
$v_0=(9\times10^{4}),$
we conclude that the equation for the velocity is

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}^{2} & =\frac{2\cdot 16\cdot (8\times {10}^{5})^{2}}{r}+(9\times {10}^{4})^{2}-2\cdot 16\cdot (8\times {10}^{5}) \\  & =\frac{2048\times {10}^{10}}{r}+(81\times {10}^{8})-(256\times {10}^{5}) \\  & =\frac{2.048\times {10}^{13}}{r}+(8.1\times {10}^{9})-(0.0256\times {10}^{9}) \\  & =\frac{2.048\times {10}^{13}}{r}+((8.1-0.0256)\times {10}^{9}) \\  & =\frac{2.048\times {10}^{13}}{r}+(8.0744\times {10}^{9}).\end{aligned}
$$

e-21750.problem:
Consider a planet with radius $(1.2\times10^{8})\,\textrm{m}$ and surface gravitational acceleration $g = 18.9\,\textrm{m/s}^2.$
What is the escape velocity of an object launched radially outward from the planet's surface? Assume only the force due to gravity acts on the object, 

Express your answer in scientific notation, rounding to **three significant figures** where appropriate.
e-21750.worked_solution:
Escape velocity is the minimum launch speed from a planet’s surface required to escape its gravity and reach infinity, neglecting all forces except gravity.

Let $R$ be the planet's radius and $g$ be the planet's surface gravitational acceleration.

According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, the magnitude of the inward gravitational force pulling the object toward the planet is

$$
F_\text{in} = G\,\dfrac{mM}{r^2},
$$

where $G$ is the gravitational constant, $m$ is the object's mass, $M$ is the planet's mass, and $r$ is the distance from the planet's center to the object.

Since this is the only force and it acts inward, the resultant force, taking *outward* as positive, is $F=-F_\textrm{in}.$
Applying Newton's second law, $F=ma,$ where $a$ is the acceleration of the object, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =-{F}_{\text{in}} \\ ma & =-G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}} \\ a & =-\frac{GM}{{r}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the acceleration is inversely proportional to the square of the distance, 

$$
a=-\dfrac{k}{r^2},
$$

 with constant of proportionality $k=GM > 0.$

When at the surface, $r=R,$ the acceleration of the object due to gravity is $a=-g.$ Substituting into our previous equation, we can solve for $k{:}$

$$
-g = -\dfrac{k}{R^2} 
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
k = gR^2
$$

Substituting back into the equation, we get

$$
a = -\dfrac{gR^2}{r^2}.
$$

Now, since acceleration $a$ is the derivative of velocity $v,$ which is the derivative of distance $r,$ we can express acceleration as follows using the chain rule, treating $v$ as a function of $r$ along the trajectory:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{dv}{dt} \\  & =\frac{dr}{dt}\cdot \frac{dv}{dr} \\  & =v\frac{dv}{dr}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this result into our equation, we obtain a separable differential equation for the velocity:

$$
v\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}r} = -\dfrac{gR^2}{r^2}
$$

Solving using separation of variables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int v\frac{dv}{dr}\,dr & =\int (-\frac{g{R}^{2}}{{r}^{2}})\,dr \\ \int v\,dv & =-g{R}^{2}\int \frac{1}{{r}^{2}}\,dr \\ \frac{{v}^{2}}{2} & =-g{R}^{2}(-\frac{1}{r})+{C}_{1} \\ {v}^{2} & =\frac{2g{R}^{2}}{r}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $C=2C_1$ is a constant of integration.

Let $v_0$ be the initial velocity of the object. Applying the initial condition $v(R) = v_0,$ we can solve for $C{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(R)^{2} & =\frac{2g{R}^{2}}{R}+C \\ {v}_{0}^{2} & =2gR+C \\ C & ={v}_{0}^{2}-2gR\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation for the velocity of the object is

$$
v^2 = \dfrac{2gR^2}{r} + v_0^2 - 2gR.
$$

For the object to escape the planet's gravity, we require a positive initial velocity, and for the velocity to never equal zero.

Notice in our velocity equation that as $r \to \infty,$ the expression $\dfrac{2gR^2}{r}$ approaches zero. So, for the velocity to never vanish, we must have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{0}^{2}-2gR & \ge 0 \\ {v}_{0}^{2} & \ge 2gR \\ {v}_{0} & \ge \sqrt{2gR}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the minimum velocity of the object to escape the surface of the planet is

$$
v_e = \sqrt{2gR}.
$$

Finally, substituting in the values $R=(1.2\times10^{8})$ and $g=18.9,$ we conclude that the escape velocity is

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{e} & =\sqrt{2\cdot (1.2\times {10}^{8})\cdot 18.9} \\  & =\sqrt{(2\cdot 1.2\cdot 18.9)\times {10}^{8}} \\  & =\sqrt{45.36}\times \sqrt{{10}^{8}} \\  & ≈(6.73\times {10}^{4})\,\text{m/s},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three significant figures.

Consider a spherical planet with radius (6.1×107)m and surface gravitational acceleration g=8.3m/s2. Which differential equation best models the velocity v of an object projected radially outward from the planet, where r is the distance from the planet's center to the object? Assume the only force acting on the object is the force due to gravity.

a
vdvdr=−3.30000×1016r2
b
dvdr=−3.00000×1014r2
c
dvdr=−3.08843×1016r2
d
vdvdr=−3.08843×1016r2
e
vdvdr=−3.00000×1016r2

decision.explanation: Gravity gives a=-gR^2/r^2, where gR^2=8.3(6.1×10^7)^2=3.08843×10^16. By the chain rule, a=dv/dt=(dv/dr)(dr/dt)=v dv/dr. Therefore option d is correct.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem: Consider a spherical  planet with radius $(6.1\times {10}^{7})\,\text{m}$ and surface gravitational acceleration $g=8.3\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$ Which differential equation best models the velocity $v$ of an object projected radially outward from the planet, where $r$ is the distance from the planet's center to the object? Assume the only force acting on the object is the force due to gravity.
after.worked_solution:
According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, the magnitude of the inward gravitational force pulling the object toward the planet is

$$
{F}_{\text{in}}=G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}},
$$

where $G$ is the gravitational constant, $m$ is the object's mass, and $M$ is the planet's mass.

Since this is the only force and it acts inward, the resultant force, taking *outward* as positive, is $F=-{F}_{\text{in}}.$
Applying Newton's second law, $F=ma,$ where $a$ is the acceleration of the object, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =-{F}_{\text{in}} \\ ma & =-G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}} \\ a & =-\frac{GM}{{r}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the acceleration is inversely proportional to the square of the distance,

$$
a=-\frac{k}{{r}^{2}},
$$

with constant of proportionality $k=GM>0.$

When at the surface, $r=(6.1\times {10}^{7})\,\text{m},$ the acceleration of the object due to gravity is $a=-8.3\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$ Substituting into our previous equation, we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-8.3 & =-\frac{k}{(6.1\times {10}^{7})^{2}} \\ k & =8.3\cdot (6.1\times {10}^{7})^{2} \\  & =8.3\cdot (6.1)^{2}\times ({10}^{7})^{2} \\  & =308.843\times {10}^{14} \\  & =3.08843\times {10}^{16}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting back into the equation, we get

$$
a=-\frac{3.08843\times {10}^{16}}{{r}^{2}}.
$$

Finally, since acceleration $a$ is the derivative of velocity $v,$ which is the derivative of distance $r,$ we can express acceleration as follows using the chain rule, treating $v$ as a function of $r$ along the trajectory:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{dv}{dt} \\  & =\frac{dr}{dt}\cdot \frac{dv}{dr} \\  & =v\frac{dv}{dr}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, substituting this result into our equation, we obtain a separable differential equation for the velocity:

$$
v\frac{dv}{dr}=-\frac{3.08843\times {10}^{16}}{{r}^{2}}
$$

Question 1
?

Consider a spherical planet with radius (6.1×107)m and surface gravitational acceleration g=8.3m/s2. Which differential equation best models the velocity v of an object projected radially outward from the planet, where r is the distance from the planet's center to the object? Assume the only force acting on the object is the force due to gravity.

a
vdvdr=−3.30000×1016r2
b
dvdr=−3.00000×1014r2
c
dvdr=−3.08843×1016r2
d
vdvdr=−3.08843×1016r2
e
vdvdr=−3.00000×1016r2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, the magnitude of the inward gravitational force pulling the object toward the planet is

Fin=GmMr2,

where G is the gravitational constant, m is the object's mass, and M is the planet's mass.

Since this is the only force and it acts inward, the resultant force, taking outward as positive, is F=−Fin. Applying Newton's second law, F=ma, where a is the acceleration of the object, we have

F=−Finma=−GmMr2a=−GMr2.

In other words, the acceleration is inversely proportional to the square of the distance, a=−kr2, with constant of proportionality k=GM>0.

When at the surface, r=(6.1×107)m, the acceleration of the object due to gravity is a=−8.3m/s2. Substituting into our previous equation, we can solve for k:

−8.3=−k(6.1×107)2k=8.3⋅(6.1×107)2=8.3⋅(6.1)2×(107)2=308.843×1014=3.08843×1016

Substituting back into the equation, we get

a=−3.08843×1016r2.

Finally, since acceleration a is the derivative of velocity v, which is the derivative of distance r, we can express acceleration as follows using the chain rule, treating v as a function of r along the trajectory:

a=dvdt=drdt⋅dvdr=vdvdr

Therefore, substituting this result into our equation, we obtain a separable differential equation for the velocity:

vdvdr=−3.08843×1016r2

content.problem: Consider a spherical  planet with radius $(6.1\times {10}^{7})\,\text{m}$ and surface gravitational acceleration $g=8.3\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$ Which differential equation best models the velocity $v$ of an object projected radially outward from the planet, where $r$ is the distance from the planet's center to the object? Assume the only force acting on the object is the force due to gravity.
content.worked_solution:
According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, the magnitude of the inward gravitational force pulling the object toward the planet is

$$
{F}_{\text{in}}=G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}},
$$

where $G$ is the gravitational constant, $m$ is the object's mass, and $M$ is the planet's mass.

Since this is the only force and it acts inward, the resultant force, taking *outward* as positive, is $F=-{F}_{\text{in}}.$
Applying Newton's second law, $F=ma,$ where $a$ is the acceleration of the object, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =-{F}_{\text{in}} \\ ma & =-G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}} \\ a & =-\frac{GM}{{r}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the acceleration is inversely proportional to the square of the distance,

$$
a=-\frac{k}{{r}^{2}},
$$

with constant of proportionality $k=GM>0.$

When at the surface, $r=(6.1\times {10}^{7})\,\text{m},$ the acceleration of the object due to gravity is $a=-8.3\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$ Substituting into our previous equation, we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-8.3 & =-\frac{k}{(6.1\times {10}^{7})^{2}} \\ k & =8.3\cdot (6.1\times {10}^{7})^{2} \\  & =8.3\cdot (6.1)^{2}\times ({10}^{7})^{2} \\  & =308.843\times {10}^{14} \\  & =3.08843\times {10}^{16}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting back into the equation, we get

$$
a=-\frac{3.08843\times {10}^{16}}{{r}^{2}}.
$$

Finally, since acceleration $a$ is the derivative of velocity $v,$ which is the derivative of distance $r,$ we can express acceleration as follows using the chain rule, treating $v$ as a function of $r$ along the trajectory:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{dv}{dt} \\  & =\frac{dr}{dt}\cdot \frac{dv}{dr} \\  & =v\frac{dv}{dr}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, substituting this result into our equation, we obtain a separable differential equation for the velocity:

$$
v\frac{dv}{dr}=-\frac{3.08843\times {10}^{16}}{{r}^{2}}
$$

Question 2

Consider a spherical icy moon with radius (6.2×104)m and surface gravitational acceleration g=9.5m/s2. Which differential equation best models the velocity v of an object projected radially outward from the icy moon, where r is the distance from the icy moon's center to the object? Assume the only force acting on the object is the force due to gravity.

a
dvdr=−3.6518×1010r2
b
vdvdr=−3.8000×1010r2
c
dvdr=−3.5500×1010r2
d
vdvdr=−3.5500×1010r2
e
vdvdr=−3.6518×1010r2
Submit

decision.explanation: The gravitational acceleration is a=-gR^2/r^2, with gR^2=9.5(6.2×10^4)^2=3.6518×10^10. The chain rule gives a=dv/dt=v dv/dr, so option e is correct.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: Consider a spherical icy moon with radius $(6.2\times {10}^{4})\,\text{m}$ and surface gravitational acceleration $g=9.5\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$ Which differential equation best models the velocity $v$ of an object projected radially outward from the icy moon, where $r$ is the distance from the icy moon's center to the object? Assume the only force acting on the object is the force due to gravity.
after.worked_solution:
According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, the magnitude of the inward gravitational force pulling the object toward the icy moon is

$$
{F}_{\text{in}}=G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}},
$$

where $G$ is the gravitational constant, $m$ is the object's mass, and $M$ is the icy moon's mass.

Since this is the only force and it acts inward, the resultant force, taking *outward* as positive, is $F=-{F}_{\text{in}}.$
Applying Newton's second law, $F=ma,$ where $a$ is the acceleration of the object, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =-{F}_{\text{in}} \\ ma & =-G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}} \\ a & =-\frac{GM}{{r}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the acceleration is inversely proportional to the square of the distance,

$$
a=-\frac{k}{{r}^{2}},
$$

with constant of proportionality $k=GM>0.$

When at the surface, $r=(6.2\times {10}^{4})\,\text{m},$ the acceleration of the object due to gravity is $a=-9.5\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$ Substituting into our previous equation, we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-9.5 & =-\frac{k}{(6.2\times {10}^{4})^{2}} \\ k & =9.5\cdot (6.2\times {10}^{4})^{2} \\  & =9.5\cdot (6.2)^{2}\times ({10}^{4})^{2} \\  & =365.18\times {10}^{8} \\  & =3.6518\times {10}^{10}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting back into the equation, we get

$$
a=-\frac{3.6518\times {10}^{10}}{{r}^{2}}.
$$

Finally, since acceleration $a$ is the derivative of velocity $v,$ which is the derivative of distance $r,$ we can express acceleration as follows using the chain rule, treating $v$ as a function of $r$ along the trajectory:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{dv}{dt} \\  & =\frac{dr}{dt}\cdot \frac{dv}{dr} \\  & =v\frac{dv}{dr}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, substituting this result into our equation, we obtain a separable differential equation for the velocity:

$$
v\frac{dv}{dr}=-\frac{3.6518\times {10}^{10}}{{r}^{2}}
$$

Question 2
?

Consider a spherical icy moon with radius (6.2×104)m and surface gravitational acceleration g=9.5m/s2. Which differential equation best models the velocity v of an object projected radially outward from the icy moon, where r is the distance from the icy moon's center to the object? Assume the only force acting on the object is the force due to gravity.

a
dvdr=−3.6518×1010r2
b
vdvdr=−3.8000×1010r2
c
dvdr=−3.5500×1010r2
d
vdvdr=−3.5500×1010r2
e
vdvdr=−3.6518×1010r2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, the magnitude of the inward gravitational force pulling the object toward the icy moon is

Fin=GmMr2,

where G is the gravitational constant, m is the object's mass, and M is the icy moon's mass.

Since this is the only force and it acts inward, the resultant force, taking outward as positive, is F=−Fin. Applying Newton's second law, F=ma, where a is the acceleration of the object, we have

F=−Finma=−GmMr2a=−GMr2.

In other words, the acceleration is inversely proportional to the square of the distance, a=−kr2, with constant of proportionality k=GM>0.

When at the surface, r=(6.2×104)m, the acceleration of the object due to gravity is a=−9.5m/s2. Substituting into our previous equation, we can solve for k:

−9.5=−k(6.2×104)2k=9.5⋅(6.2×104)2=9.5⋅(6.2)2×(104)2=365.18×108=3.6518×1010

Substituting back into the equation, we get

a=−3.6518×1010r2.

Finally, since acceleration a is the derivative of velocity v, which is the derivative of distance r, we can express acceleration as follows using the chain rule, treating v as a function of r along the trajectory:

a=dvdt=drdt⋅dvdr=vdvdr

Therefore, substituting this result into our equation, we obtain a separable differential equation for the velocity:

vdvdr=−3.6518×1010r2

content.problem: Consider a spherical icy moon with radius $(6.2\times {10}^{4})\,\text{m}$ and surface gravitational acceleration $g=9.5\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$ Which differential equation best models the velocity $v$ of an object projected radially outward from the icy moon, where $r$ is the distance from the icy moon's center to the object? Assume the only force acting on the object is the force due to gravity.
content.worked_solution:
According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, the magnitude of the inward gravitational force pulling the object toward the icy moon is

$$
{F}_{\text{in}}=G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}},
$$

where $G$ is the gravitational constant, $m$ is the object's mass, and $M$ is the icy moon's mass.

Since this is the only force and it acts inward, the resultant force, taking *outward* as positive, is $F=-{F}_{\text{in}}.$
Applying Newton's second law, $F=ma,$ where $a$ is the acceleration of the object, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =-{F}_{\text{in}} \\ ma & =-G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}} \\ a & =-\frac{GM}{{r}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the acceleration is inversely proportional to the square of the distance,

$$
a=-\frac{k}{{r}^{2}},
$$

with constant of proportionality $k=GM>0.$

When at the surface, $r=(6.2\times {10}^{4})\,\text{m},$ the acceleration of the object due to gravity is $a=-9.5\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$ Substituting into our previous equation, we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-9.5 & =-\frac{k}{(6.2\times {10}^{4})^{2}} \\ k & =9.5\cdot (6.2\times {10}^{4})^{2} \\  & =9.5\cdot (6.2)^{2}\times ({10}^{4})^{2} \\  & =365.18\times {10}^{8} \\  & =3.6518\times {10}^{10}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting back into the equation, we get

$$
a=-\frac{3.6518\times {10}^{10}}{{r}^{2}}.
$$

Finally, since acceleration $a$ is the derivative of velocity $v,$ which is the derivative of distance $r,$ we can express acceleration as follows using the chain rule, treating $v$ as a function of $r$ along the trajectory:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{dv}{dt} \\  & =\frac{dr}{dt}\cdot \frac{dv}{dr} \\  & =v\frac{dv}{dr}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, substituting this result into our equation, we obtain a separable differential equation for the velocity:

$$
v\frac{dv}{dr}=-\frac{3.6518\times {10}^{10}}{{r}^{2}}
$$

Question 3
?

Consider a spherical exoplanet with radius (7×107)m and surface gravitational acceleration g=8m/s2. Which differential equation best models the velocity v of an object projected radially outward from the exoplanet, where r is the distance from the exoplanet's center to the object? Assume the only force acting on the object is the force due to gravity.

a
vdvdr=−4.10×1016r2
b
dvdr=−3.80×1016r2
c
vdvdr=−3.80×1016r2
d
vdvdr=−3.92×1016r2
e
dvdr=−3.92×1016r2
Submit

decision.explanation: Gravity gives a=-gR^2/r^2, where gR^2=8(7×10^7)^2=3.92×10^16. Since a=dv/dt=v dv/dr by the chain rule, the correct equation is option d.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem: Consider a spherical exoplanet with radius $(7\times {10}^{7})\,\text{m}$ and surface gravitational acceleration $g=8\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$ Which differential equation best models the velocity $v$ of an object projected radially outward from the exoplanet, where $r$ is the distance from the exoplanet's center to the object? Assume the only force acting on the object is the force due to gravity.
after.worked_solution:
According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, the magnitude of the inward gravitational force pulling the object toward the exoplanet is

$$
{F}_{\text{in}}=G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}},
$$

where $G$ is the gravitational constant, $m$ is the object's mass, and $M$ is the exoplanet's mass.

Since this is the only force and it acts inward, the resultant force, taking *outward* as positive, is $F=-{F}_{\text{in}}.$
Applying Newton's second law, $F=ma,$ where $a$ is the acceleration of the object, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =-{F}_{\text{in}} \\ ma & =-G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}} \\ a & =-\frac{GM}{{r}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the acceleration is inversely proportional to the square of the distance,

$$
a=-\frac{k}{{r}^{2}},
$$

with constant of proportionality $k=GM>0.$

When at the surface, $r=(7\times {10}^{7})\,\text{m},$ the acceleration of the object due to gravity is $a=-8\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$ Substituting into our previous equation, we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-8 & =-\frac{k}{(7\times {10}^{7})^{2}} \\ k & =8\cdot (7\times {10}^{7})^{2} \\  & =8\cdot (7)^{2}\times ({10}^{7})^{2} \\  & =392\times {10}^{14} \\  & =3.92\times {10}^{16}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting back into the equation, we get

$$
a=-\frac{3.92\times {10}^{16}}{{r}^{2}}.
$$

Finally, since acceleration $a$ is the derivative of velocity $v,$ which is the derivative of distance $r,$ we can express acceleration as follows using the chain rule, treating $v$ as a function of $r$ along the trajectory:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{dv}{dt} \\  & =\frac{dr}{dt}\cdot \frac{dv}{dr} \\  & =v\frac{dv}{dr}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, substituting this result into our equation, we obtain a separable differential equation for the velocity:

$$
v\frac{dv}{dr}=-\frac{3.92\times {10}^{16}}{{r}^{2}}
$$

Question 3
?

Consider a spherical exoplanet with radius (7×107)m and surface gravitational acceleration g=8m/s2. Which differential equation best models the velocity v of an object projected radially outward from the exoplanet, where r is the distance from the exoplanet's center to the object? Assume the only force acting on the object is the force due to gravity.

a
vdvdr=−4.10×1016r2
b
dvdr=−3.80×1016r2
c
vdvdr=−3.80×1016r2
d
vdvdr=−3.92×1016r2
e
dvdr=−3.92×1016r2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, the magnitude of the inward gravitational force pulling the object toward the exoplanet is

Fin=GmMr2,

where G is the gravitational constant, m is the object's mass, and M is the exoplanet's mass.

Since this is the only force and it acts inward, the resultant force, taking outward as positive, is F=−Fin. Applying Newton's second law, F=ma, where a is the acceleration of the object, we have

F=−Finma=−GmMr2a=−GMr2.

In other words, the acceleration is inversely proportional to the square of the distance, a=−kr2, with constant of proportionality k=GM>0.

When at the surface, r=(7×107)m, the acceleration of the object due to gravity is a=−8m/s2. Substituting into our previous equation, we can solve for k:

−8=−k(7×107)2k=8⋅(7×107)2=8⋅(7)2×(107)2=392×1014=3.92×1016

Substituting back into the equation, we get

a=−3.92×1016r2.

Finally, since acceleration a is the derivative of velocity v, which is the derivative of distance r, we can express acceleration as follows using the chain rule, treating v as a function of r along the trajectory:

a=dvdt=drdt⋅dvdr=vdvdr

Therefore, substituting this result into our equation, we obtain a separable differential equation for the velocity:

vdvdr=−3.92×1016r2

content.problem: Consider a spherical exoplanet with radius $(7\times {10}^{7})\,\text{m}$ and surface gravitational acceleration $g=8\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$ Which differential equation best models the velocity $v$ of an object projected radially outward from the exoplanet, where $r$ is the distance from the exoplanet's center to the object? Assume the only force acting on the object is the force due to gravity.
content.worked_solution:
According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, the magnitude of the inward gravitational force pulling the object toward the exoplanet is

$$
{F}_{\text{in}}=G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}},
$$

where $G$ is the gravitational constant, $m$ is the object's mass, and $M$ is the exoplanet's mass.

Since this is the only force and it acts inward, the resultant force, taking *outward* as positive, is $F=-{F}_{\text{in}}.$
Applying Newton's second law, $F=ma,$ where $a$ is the acceleration of the object, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =-{F}_{\text{in}} \\ ma & =-G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}} \\ a & =-\frac{GM}{{r}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the acceleration is inversely proportional to the square of the distance,

$$
a=-\frac{k}{{r}^{2}},
$$

with constant of proportionality $k=GM>0.$

When at the surface, $r=(7\times {10}^{7})\,\text{m},$ the acceleration of the object due to gravity is $a=-8\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$ Substituting into our previous equation, we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-8 & =-\frac{k}{(7\times {10}^{7})^{2}} \\ k & =8\cdot (7\times {10}^{7})^{2} \\  & =8\cdot (7)^{2}\times ({10}^{7})^{2} \\  & =392\times {10}^{14} \\  & =3.92\times {10}^{16}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting back into the equation, we get

$$
a=-\frac{3.92\times {10}^{16}}{{r}^{2}}.
$$

Finally, since acceleration $a$ is the derivative of velocity $v,$ which is the derivative of distance $r,$ we can express acceleration as follows using the chain rule, treating $v$ as a function of $r$ along the trajectory:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{dv}{dt} \\  & =\frac{dr}{dt}\cdot \frac{dv}{dr} \\  & =v\frac{dv}{dr}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, substituting this result into our equation, we obtain a separable differential equation for the velocity:

$$
v\frac{dv}{dr}=-\frac{3.92\times {10}^{16}}{{r}^{2}}
$$

Question 4
?

Consider a spherical giant moon with radius (5.9×1011)m and surface gravitational acceleration g=9.2m/s2. Which differential equation best models the velocity v of an object projected radially outward from the giant moon, where r is the distance from the giant moon's center to the object? Assume the only force acting on the object is the force due to gravity.

a
dvdr=−3.10×1014r2
b
dvdr=−3.20252×1024r2
c
vdvdr=−3.40×1024r2
d
vdvdr=−3.10×1024r2
e
vdvdr=−3.20252×1024r2
Submit

decision.explanation: Gravity gives a=-gR^2/r^2, with gR^2=9.2(5.9×10^11)^2=3.20252×10^24. By the chain rule, a=dv/dt=v dv/dr. Thus option e is correct.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem: Consider a spherical giant moon with radius $(5.9\times {10}^{11})\,\text{m}$ and surface gravitational acceleration $g=9.2\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$ Which differential equation best models the velocity $v$ of an object projected radially outward from the  giant moon, where $r$ is the distance from the giant moon's center to the object? Assume the only force acting on the object is the force due to gravity.
after.worked_solution:
According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, the magnitude of the inward gravitational force pulling the object toward the giant moon is

$$
{F}_{\text{in}}=G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}},
$$

where $G$ is the gravitational constant, $m$ is the object's mass, and $M$ is the giant moon's mass.

Since this is the only force and it acts inward, the resultant force, taking *outward* as positive, is $F=-{F}_{\text{in}}.$
Applying Newton's second law, $F=ma,$ where $a$ is the acceleration of the object, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =-{F}_{\text{in}} \\ ma & =-G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}} \\ a & =-\frac{GM}{{r}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the acceleration is inversely proportional to the square of the distance,

$$
a=-\frac{k}{{r}^{2}},
$$

with constant of proportionality $k=GM>0.$

When at the surface, $r=(5.9\times {10}^{11})\,\text{m},$ the acceleration of the object due to gravity is $a=-9.2\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$ Substituting into our previous equation, we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-9.2 & =-\frac{k}{(5.9\times {10}^{11})^{2}} \\ k & =9.2\cdot (5.9\times {10}^{11})^{2} \\  & =9.2\cdot (5.9)^{2}\times ({10}^{11})^{2} \\  & =320.252\times {10}^{22} \\  & =3.20252\times {10}^{24}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting back into the equation, we get

$$
a=-\frac{3.20252\times {10}^{24}}{{r}^{2}}.
$$

Finally, since acceleration $a$ is the derivative of velocity $v,$ which is the derivative of distance $r,$ we can express acceleration as follows using the chain rule, treating $v$ as a function of $r$ along the trajectory:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{dv}{dt} \\  & =\frac{dr}{dt}\cdot \frac{dv}{dr} \\  & =v\frac{dv}{dr}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, substituting this result into our equation, we obtain a separable differential equation for the velocity:

$$
v\frac{dv}{dr}=-\frac{3.20252\times {10}^{24}}{{r}^{2}}
$$

Question 4
?

Consider a spherical giant moon with radius (5.9×1011)m and surface gravitational acceleration g=9.2m/s2. Which differential equation best models the velocity v of an object projected radially outward from the giant moon, where r is the distance from the giant moon's center to the object? Assume the only force acting on the object is the force due to gravity.

a
dvdr=−3.10×1014r2
b
dvdr=−3.20252×1024r2
c
vdvdr=−3.40×1024r2
d
vdvdr=−3.10×1024r2
e
vdvdr=−3.20252×1024r2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, the magnitude of the inward gravitational force pulling the object toward the giant moon is

Fin=GmMr2,

where G is the gravitational constant, m is the object's mass, and M is the giant moon's mass.

Since this is the only force and it acts inward, the resultant force, taking outward as positive, is F=−Fin. Applying Newton's second law, F=ma, where a is the acceleration of the object, we have

F=−Finma=−GmMr2a=−GMr2.

In other words, the acceleration is inversely proportional to the square of the distance, a=−kr2, with constant of proportionality k=GM>0.

When at the surface, r=(5.9×1011)m, the acceleration of the object due to gravity is a=−9.2m/s2. Substituting into our previous equation, we can solve for k:

−9.2=−k(5.9×1011)2k=9.2⋅(5.9×1011)2=9.2⋅(5.9)2×(1011)2=320.252×1022=3.20252×1024

Substituting back into the equation, we get

a=−3.20252×1024r2.

Finally, since acceleration a is the derivative of velocity v, which is the derivative of distance r, we can express acceleration as follows using the chain rule, treating v as a function of r along the trajectory:

a=dvdt=drdt⋅dvdr=vdvdr

Therefore, substituting this result into our equation, we obtain a separable differential equation for the velocity:

vdvdr=−3.20252×1024r2

content.problem: Consider a spherical giant moon with radius $(5.9\times {10}^{11})\,\text{m}$ and surface gravitational acceleration $g=9.2\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$ Which differential equation best models the velocity $v$ of an object projected radially outward from the  giant moon, where $r$ is the distance from the giant moon's center to the object? Assume the only force acting on the object is the force due to gravity.
content.worked_solution:
According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, the magnitude of the inward gravitational force pulling the object toward the giant moon is

$$
{F}_{\text{in}}=G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}},
$$

where $G$ is the gravitational constant, $m$ is the object's mass, and $M$ is the giant moon's mass.

Since this is the only force and it acts inward, the resultant force, taking *outward* as positive, is $F=-{F}_{\text{in}}.$
Applying Newton's second law, $F=ma,$ where $a$ is the acceleration of the object, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =-{F}_{\text{in}} \\ ma & =-G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}} \\ a & =-\frac{GM}{{r}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the acceleration is inversely proportional to the square of the distance,

$$
a=-\frac{k}{{r}^{2}},
$$

with constant of proportionality $k=GM>0.$

When at the surface, $r=(5.9\times {10}^{11})\,\text{m},$ the acceleration of the object due to gravity is $a=-9.2\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$ Substituting into our previous equation, we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-9.2 & =-\frac{k}{(5.9\times {10}^{11})^{2}} \\ k & =9.2\cdot (5.9\times {10}^{11})^{2} \\  & =9.2\cdot (5.9)^{2}\times ({10}^{11})^{2} \\  & =320.252\times {10}^{22} \\  & =3.20252\times {10}^{24}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting back into the equation, we get

$$
a=-\frac{3.20252\times {10}^{24}}{{r}^{2}}.
$$

Finally, since acceleration $a$ is the derivative of velocity $v,$ which is the derivative of distance $r,$ we can express acceleration as follows using the chain rule, treating $v$ as a function of $r$ along the trajectory:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{dv}{dt} \\  & =\frac{dr}{dt}\cdot \frac{dv}{dr} \\  & =v\frac{dv}{dr}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, substituting this result into our equation, we obtain a separable differential equation for the velocity:

$$
v\frac{dv}{dr}=-\frac{3.20252\times {10}^{24}}{{r}^{2}}
$$

Consider a spherical rocky planet with radius (5.8×104)m and surface gravitational acceleration g=7.5m/s2. Which differential equation best models the velocity v of an object projected radially outward from the rocky planet, where r is the distance from the rocky planet's center to the object? Assume the only force acting on the object is the force due to gravity.

a
vdvdr=−2.523×1010r2
b
dvdr=−2.400×1010r2
c
dvdr=−2.523×1010r2
d
vdvdr=−2.700×1010r2
e
vdvdr=−2.400×1010r2

decision.explanation: Gravity gives a=-gR^2/r^2, where gR^2=7.5(5.8×10^4)^2=2.523×10^10. The chain rule gives a=dv/dt=v dv/dr, so option a is correct.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem: Consider a spherical rocky planet with radius $(5.8\times {10}^{4})\,\text{m}$ and surface gravitational acceleration $g=7.5\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$ Which differential equation best models the velocity $v$ of an object projected radially outward from the rocky planet, where $r$ is the distance from the rocky planet's center to the object? Assume the only force acting on the object is the force due to gravity.
after.worked_solution:
According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, the magnitude of the inward gravitational force pulling the object toward the rocky planet is

$$
{F}_{\text{in}}=G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}},
$$

where $G$ is the gravitational constant, $m$ is the object's mass, and $M$ is the rocky planet's mass.

Since this is the only force and it acts inward, the resultant force, taking *outward* as positive, is $F=-{F}_{\text{in}}.$
Applying Newton's second law, $F=ma,$ where $a$ is the acceleration of the object, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =-{F}_{\text{in}} \\ ma & =-G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}} \\ a & =-\frac{GM}{{r}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the acceleration is inversely proportional to the square of the distance,

$$
a=-\frac{k}{{r}^{2}},
$$

with constant of proportionality $k=GM>0.$

When at the surface, $r=(5.8\times {10}^{4})\,\text{m},$ the acceleration of the object due to gravity is $a=-7.5\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$ Substituting into our previous equation, we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-7.5 & =-\frac{k}{(5.8\times {10}^{4})^{2}} \\ k & =7.5\cdot (5.8\times {10}^{4})^{2} \\  & =7.5\cdot (5.8)^{2}\times ({10}^{4})^{2} \\  & =252.3\times {10}^{8} \\  & =2.523\times {10}^{10}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting back into the equation, we get

$$
a=-\frac{2.523\times {10}^{10}}{{r}^{2}}.
$$

Finally, since acceleration $a$ is the derivative of velocity $v,$ which is the derivative of distance $r,$ we can express acceleration as follows using the chain rule, treating $v$ as a function of $r$ along the trajectory:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{dv}{dt} \\  & =\frac{dr}{dt}\cdot \frac{dv}{dr} \\  & =v\frac{dv}{dr}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, substituting this result into our equation, we obtain a separable differential equation for the velocity:

$$
v\frac{dv}{dr}=-\frac{2.523\times {10}^{10}}{{r}^{2}}
$$

Question 5
?

Consider a spherical rocky planet with radius (5.8×104)m and surface gravitational acceleration g=7.5m/s2. Which differential equation best models the velocity v of an object projected radially outward from the rocky planet, where r is the distance from the rocky planet's center to the object? Assume the only force acting on the object is the force due to gravity.

a
vdvdr=−2.523×1010r2
b
dvdr=−2.400×1010r2
c
dvdr=−2.523×1010r2
d
vdvdr=−2.700×1010r2
e
vdvdr=−2.400×1010r2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, the magnitude of the inward gravitational force pulling the object toward the rocky planet is

Fin=GmMr2,

where G is the gravitational constant, m is the object's mass, and M is the rocky planet's mass.

Since this is the only force and it acts inward, the resultant force, taking outward as positive, is F=−Fin. Applying Newton's second law, F=ma, where a is the acceleration of the object, we have

F=−Finma=−GmMr2a=−GMr2.

In other words, the acceleration is inversely proportional to the square of the distance, a=−kr2, with constant of proportionality k=GM>0.

When at the surface, r=(5.8×104)m, the acceleration of the object due to gravity is a=−7.5m/s2. Substituting into our previous equation, we can solve for k:

−7.5=−k(5.8×104)2k=7.5⋅(5.8×104)2=7.5⋅(5.8)2×(104)2=252.3×108=2.523×1010

Substituting back into the equation, we get

a=−2.523×1010r2.

Finally, since acceleration a is the derivative of velocity v, which is the derivative of distance r, we can express acceleration as follows using the chain rule, treating v as a function of r along the trajectory:

a=dvdt=drdt⋅dvdr=vdvdr

Therefore, substituting this result into our equation, we obtain a separable differential equation for the velocity:

vdvdr=−2.523×1010r2

content.problem: Consider a spherical rocky planet with radius $(5.8\times {10}^{4})\,\text{m}$ and surface gravitational acceleration $g=7.5\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$ Which differential equation best models the velocity $v$ of an object projected radially outward from the rocky planet, where $r$ is the distance from the rocky planet's center to the object? Assume the only force acting on the object is the force due to gravity.
content.worked_solution:
According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, the magnitude of the inward gravitational force pulling the object toward the rocky planet is

$$
{F}_{\text{in}}=G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}},
$$

where $G$ is the gravitational constant, $m$ is the object's mass, and $M$ is the rocky planet's mass.

Since this is the only force and it acts inward, the resultant force, taking *outward* as positive, is $F=-{F}_{\text{in}}.$
Applying Newton's second law, $F=ma,$ where $a$ is the acceleration of the object, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =-{F}_{\text{in}} \\ ma & =-G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}} \\ a & =-\frac{GM}{{r}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the acceleration is inversely proportional to the square of the distance,

$$
a=-\frac{k}{{r}^{2}},
$$

with constant of proportionality $k=GM>0.$

When at the surface, $r=(5.8\times {10}^{4})\,\text{m},$ the acceleration of the object due to gravity is $a=-7.5\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$ Substituting into our previous equation, we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-7.5 & =-\frac{k}{(5.8\times {10}^{4})^{2}} \\ k & =7.5\cdot (5.8\times {10}^{4})^{2} \\  & =7.5\cdot (5.8)^{2}\times ({10}^{4})^{2} \\  & =252.3\times {10}^{8} \\  & =2.523\times {10}^{10}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting back into the equation, we get

$$
a=-\frac{2.523\times {10}^{10}}{{r}^{2}}.
$$

Finally, since acceleration $a$ is the derivative of velocity $v,$ which is the derivative of distance $r,$ we can express acceleration as follows using the chain rule, treating $v$ as a function of $r$ along the trajectory:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{dv}{dt} \\  & =\frac{dr}{dt}\cdot \frac{dv}{dr} \\  & =v\frac{dv}{dr}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, substituting this result into our equation, we obtain a separable differential equation for the velocity:

$$
v\frac{dv}{dr}=-\frac{2.523\times {10}^{10}}{{r}^{2}}
$$

before.html:
Question 6
?

Consider a spherical planet with radius (2×107)m and surface gravitational acceleration g=20m/s2. Which equation best models the velocity v of an object projected radially outward from the planet's surface with an initial velocity of (6×104)m/s, where r is the distance from the planet's center to the object. Assume the only force acting on the object is the force due to gravity.

a
v2=1.6×1016r−(2.8×109)
b
v2=1.6×1016r+(2.8×109)
c
v2=0.8×1016r−(3.6×109)
d
v2=0.8×1016r+(2.8×109)
e
v2=1.6×1016r2+(3.6×109)
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating v dv/dr=-gR^2/r^2 gives v^2=2gR^2/r+v_0^2-2gR. Here 2gR^2=1.6×10^16 and v_0^2-2gR=3.6×10^9-0.8×10^9=2.8×10^9, so option b is correct.

after.name: Question 6
after.problem: Consider a spherical planet with radius $(2\times {10}^{7})\,\text{m}$ and surface gravitational acceleration $g=20\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$ Which equation best models the velocity $v$ of an object projected radially outward from the planet's surface with an initial velocity of $(6\times {10}^{4})\,\text{m/s},$ where $r$ is the distance from the planet's center to the object. Assume the only force acting on the object is the force due to gravity.
after.worked_solution:
Let $R$ be the planet's radius and $g$ be the planet's surface gravitational acceleration.

According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, the magnitude of the inward gravitational force pulling the object toward the planet is

$$
{F}_{\text{in}}=G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}},
$$

where $G$ is the gravitational constant, $m$ is the object's mass, and $M$ is the planet's mass.

Since this is the only force and it acts inward, the resultant force, taking *outward* as positive, is $F=-{F}_{\text{in}}.$
Applying Newton's second law, $F=ma,$ where $a$ is the acceleration of the object, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =-{F}_{\text{in}} \\ ma & =-G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}} \\ a & =-\frac{GM}{{r}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the acceleration is inversely proportional to the square of the distance,

$$
a=-\frac{k}{{r}^{2}},
$$

with constant of proportionality $k=GM>0.$

When at the surface, $r=R,$ the acceleration of the object due to gravity is $a=-g.$ Substituting into our previous equation, we can solve for $k:$

$$
-g=-\frac{k}{{R}^{2}}\,\,\,⟹\,k=g{R}^{2}
$$

Substituting back into the equation, we get

$$
a=-\frac{g{R}^{2}}{{r}^{2}}.
$$

Now, since acceleration $a$ is the derivative of velocity $v,$ which is the derivative of distance $r,$ we can express acceleration as follows using the chain rule, treating $v$ as a function of $r$ along the trajectory:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{dv}{dt} \\  & =\frac{dr}{dt}\cdot \frac{dv}{dr} \\  & =v\frac{dv}{dr}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this result into our equation, we obtain a separable differential equation for the velocity:

$$
v\frac{dv}{dr}=-\frac{g{R}^{2}}{{r}^{2}}
$$

Solving using separation of variables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int v\frac{dv}{dr}\,dr & =\int (-\frac{g{R}^{2}}{{r}^{2}})\,dr \\ \int v\,dv & =-g{R}^{2}\int \frac{1}{{r}^{2}}\,dr \\ \frac{{v}^{2}}{2} & =-g{R}^{2}(-\frac{1}{r})+{C}_{1} \\ {v}^{2} & =\frac{2g{R}^{2}}{r}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $C=2{C}_{1}$ is a constant of integration.

Let ${v}_{0}$ be the initial velocity of the object. Applying the initial condition $v(R)={v}_{0},$ we can solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(R)^{2} & =\frac{2g{R}^{2}}{R}+C \\ {v}_{0}^{2} & =2gR+C \\ C & ={v}_{0}^{2}-2gR\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation for the velocity of the object is

$$
{v}^{2}=\frac{2g{R}^{2}}{r}+{v}_{0}^{2}-2gR.
$$

Finally, substituting in the values
$R=(2\times {10}^{7}),$
$g=20,$ and
${v}_{0}=(6\times {10}^{4}),$
we conclude that the equation for the velocity is

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}^{2} & =\frac{2\cdot 20\cdot (2\times {10}^{7})^{2}}{r}+(6\times {10}^{4})^{2}-2\cdot 20\cdot (2\times {10}^{7}) \\  & =\frac{160\times {10}^{14}}{r}+(36\times {10}^{8})-(80\times {10}^{7}) \\  & =\frac{1.6\times {10}^{16}}{r}+(3.6\times {10}^{9})-(0.8\times {10}^{9}) \\  & =\frac{1.6\times {10}^{16}}{r}+((3.6-0.8)\times {10}^{9}) \\  & =\frac{1.6\times {10}^{16}}{r}+(2.8\times {10}^{9}).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 6
?

Consider a spherical planet with radius (2×107)m and surface gravitational acceleration g=20m/s2. Which equation best models the velocity v of an object projected radially outward from the planet's surface with an initial velocity of (6×104)m/s, where r is the distance from the planet's center to the object. Assume the only force acting on the object is the force due to gravity.

a
v2=1.6×1016r−(2.8×109)
b
v2=1.6×1016r+(2.8×109)
c
v2=0.8×1016r−(3.6×109)
d
v2=0.8×1016r+(2.8×109)
e
v2=1.6×1016r2+(3.6×109)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let R be the planet's radius and g be the planet's surface gravitational acceleration.

According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, the magnitude of the inward gravitational force pulling the object toward the planet is

Fin=GmMr2,

where G is the gravitational constant, m is the object's mass, and M is the planet's mass.

Since this is the only force and it acts inward, the resultant force, taking outward as positive, is F=−Fin. Applying Newton's second law, F=ma, where a is the acceleration of the object, we have

F=−Finma=−GmMr2a=−GMr2.

In other words, the acceleration is inversely proportional to the square of the distance, a=−kr2, with constant of proportionality k=GM>0.

When at the surface, r=R, the acceleration of the object due to gravity is a=−g. Substituting into our previous equation, we can solve for k:

−g=−kR2⟹k=gR2

Substituting back into the equation, we get

a=−gR2r2.

Now, since acceleration a is the derivative of velocity v, which is the derivative of distance r, we can express acceleration as follows using the chain rule, treating v as a function of r along the trajectory:

a=dvdt=drdt⋅dvdr=vdvdr

Substituting this result into our equation, we obtain a separable differential equation for the velocity:

vdvdr=−gR2r2

Solving using separation of variables, we have

∫vdvdrdr=∫(−gR2r2)dr∫vdv=−gR2∫1r2drv22=−gR2(−1r)+C1v2=2gR2r+C.

Note that C=2C1 is a constant of integration.

Let v0 be the initial velocity of the object. Applying the initial condition v(R)=v0, we can solve for C:

v(R)2=2gR2R+Cv02=2gR+CC=v02−2gR

Therefore, the equation for the velocity of the object is

v2=2gR2r+v02−2gR.

Finally, substituting in the values R=(2×107), g=20, and v0=(6×104), we conclude that the equation for the velocity is v2=2⋅20⋅(2×107)2r+(6×104)2−2⋅20⋅(2×107)=160×1014r+(36×108)−(80×107)=1.6×1016r+(3.6×109)−(0.8×109)=1.6×1016r+((3.6−0.8)×109)=1.6×1016r+(2.8×109).

content.knowledge_point: Solving a Radially Projected Model for Velocity
content.problem: Consider a spherical planet with radius $(2\times {10}^{7})\,\text{m}$ and surface gravitational acceleration $g=20\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$ Which equation best models the velocity $v$ of an object projected radially outward from the planet's surface with an initial velocity of $(6\times {10}^{4})\,\text{m/s},$ where $r$ is the distance from the planet's center to the object. Assume the only force acting on the object is the force due to gravity.
content.worked_solution:
Let $R$ be the planet's radius and $g$ be the planet's surface gravitational acceleration.

According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, the magnitude of the inward gravitational force pulling the object toward the planet is

$$
{F}_{\text{in}}=G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}},
$$

where $G$ is the gravitational constant, $m$ is the object's mass, and $M$ is the planet's mass.

Since this is the only force and it acts inward, the resultant force, taking *outward* as positive, is $F=-{F}_{\text{in}}.$
Applying Newton's second law, $F=ma,$ where $a$ is the acceleration of the object, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =-{F}_{\text{in}} \\ ma & =-G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}} \\ a & =-\frac{GM}{{r}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the acceleration is inversely proportional to the square of the distance,

$$
a=-\frac{k}{{r}^{2}},
$$

with constant of proportionality $k=GM>0.$

When at the surface, $r=R,$ the acceleration of the object due to gravity is $a=-g.$ Substituting into our previous equation, we can solve for $k:$

$$
-g=-\frac{k}{{R}^{2}}\,\,\,⟹\,k=g{R}^{2}
$$

Substituting back into the equation, we get

$$
a=-\frac{g{R}^{2}}{{r}^{2}}.
$$

Now, since acceleration $a$ is the derivative of velocity $v,$ which is the derivative of distance $r,$ we can express acceleration as follows using the chain rule, treating $v$ as a function of $r$ along the trajectory:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{dv}{dt} \\  & =\frac{dr}{dt}\cdot \frac{dv}{dr} \\  & =v\frac{dv}{dr}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this result into our equation, we obtain a separable differential equation for the velocity:

$$
v\frac{dv}{dr}=-\frac{g{R}^{2}}{{r}^{2}}
$$

Solving using separation of variables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int v\frac{dv}{dr}\,dr & =\int (-\frac{g{R}^{2}}{{r}^{2}})\,dr \\ \int v\,dv & =-g{R}^{2}\int \frac{1}{{r}^{2}}\,dr \\ \frac{{v}^{2}}{2} & =-g{R}^{2}(-\frac{1}{r})+{C}_{1} \\ {v}^{2} & =\frac{2g{R}^{2}}{r}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $C=2{C}_{1}$ is a constant of integration.

Let ${v}_{0}$ be the initial velocity of the object. Applying the initial condition $v(R)={v}_{0},$ we can solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(R)^{2} & =\frac{2g{R}^{2}}{R}+C \\ {v}_{0}^{2} & =2gR+C \\ C & ={v}_{0}^{2}-2gR\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation for the velocity of the object is

$$
{v}^{2}=\frac{2g{R}^{2}}{r}+{v}_{0}^{2}-2gR.
$$

Finally, substituting in the values
$R=(2\times {10}^{7}),$
$g=20,$ and
${v}_{0}=(6\times {10}^{4}),$
we conclude that the equation for the velocity is

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}^{2} & =\frac{2\cdot 20\cdot (2\times {10}^{7})^{2}}{r}+(6\times {10}^{4})^{2}-2\cdot 20\cdot (2\times {10}^{7}) \\  & =\frac{160\times {10}^{14}}{r}+(36\times {10}^{8})-(80\times {10}^{7}) \\  & =\frac{1.6\times {10}^{16}}{r}+(3.6\times {10}^{9})-(0.8\times {10}^{9}) \\  & =\frac{1.6\times {10}^{16}}{r}+((3.6-0.8)\times {10}^{9}) \\  & =\frac{1.6\times {10}^{16}}{r}+(2.8\times {10}^{9}).\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 7
?

Consider a spherical planet with radius (4×107)m and surface gravitational acceleration g=12m/s2. Which equation best models the velocity v of an object projected radially outward from the planet's surface with an initial velocity of (8×104)m/s, where r is the distance from the planet's center to the object. Assume the only force acting on the object is the force due to gravity.

a
v2=3.84×1016r−(5.44×109)
b
v2=3.84×1016r+(5.44×109)
c
v2=3.84×1016r2+(6.4×109)
d
v2=1.92×1016r+(5.44×109)
e
v2=1.92×1016r−(6.4×109)
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating v dv/dr=-gR^2/r^2 gives v^2=2gR^2/r+v_0^2-2gR. Here 2gR^2=3.84×10^16 and v_0^2-2gR=6.4×10^9-0.96×10^9=5.44×10^9. Therefore option b is correct.

after.name: Question 7
after.problem: Consider a spherical planet with radius $(4\times {10}^{7})\,\text{m}$ and surface gravitational acceleration $g=12\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$ Which equation best models the velocity $v$ of an object projected radially outward from the planet's surface with an initial velocity of $(8\times {10}^{4})\,\text{m/s},$ where $r$ is the distance from the planet's center to the object. Assume the only force acting on the object is the force due to gravity.
after.worked_solution:
Let $R$ be the planet's radius and $g$ be the planet's surface gravitational acceleration.

According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, the magnitude of the inward gravitational force pulling the object toward the planet is

$$
{F}_{\text{in}}=G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}},
$$

where $G$ is the gravitational constant, $m$ is the object's mass, and $M$ is the planet's mass.

Since this is the only force and it acts inward, the resultant force, taking *outward* as positive, is $F=-{F}_{\text{in}}.$
Applying Newton's second law, $F=ma,$ where $a$ is the acceleration of the object, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =-{F}_{\text{in}} \\ ma & =-G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}} \\ a & =-\frac{GM}{{r}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the acceleration is inversely proportional to the square of the distance,

$$
a=-\frac{k}{{r}^{2}},
$$

with constant of proportionality $k=GM>0.$

When at the surface, $r=R,$ the acceleration of the object due to gravity is $a=-g.$ Substituting into our previous equation, we can solve for $k:$

$$
-g=-\frac{k}{{R}^{2}}\,\,\,⟹\,k=g{R}^{2}
$$

Substituting back into the equation, we get

$$
a=-\frac{g{R}^{2}}{{r}^{2}}.
$$

Now, since acceleration $a$ is the derivative of velocity $v,$ which is the derivative of distance $r,$ we can express acceleration as follows using the chain rule, treating $v$ as a function of $r$ along the trajectory:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{dv}{dt} \\  & =\frac{dr}{dt}\cdot \frac{dv}{dr} \\  & =v\frac{dv}{dr}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this result into our equation, we obtain a separable differential equation for the velocity:

$$
v\frac{dv}{dr}=-\frac{g{R}^{2}}{{r}^{2}}
$$

Solving using separation of variables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int v\frac{dv}{dr}\,dr & =\int (-\frac{g{R}^{2}}{{r}^{2}})\,dr \\ \int v\,dv & =-g{R}^{2}\int \frac{1}{{r}^{2}}\,dr \\ \frac{{v}^{2}}{2} & =-g{R}^{2}(-\frac{1}{r})+{C}_{1} \\ {v}^{2} & =\frac{2g{R}^{2}}{r}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $C=2{C}_{1}$ is a constant of integration.

Let ${v}_{0}$ be the initial velocity of the object. Applying the initial condition $v(R)={v}_{0},$ we can solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(R)^{2} & =\frac{2g{R}^{2}}{R}+C \\ {v}_{0}^{2} & =2gR+C \\ C & ={v}_{0}^{2}-2gR\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation for the velocity of the object is

$$
{v}^{2}=\frac{2g{R}^{2}}{r}+{v}_{0}^{2}-2gR.
$$

Finally, substituting in the values
$R=(4\times {10}^{7}),$
$g=12,$ and
${v}_{0}=(8\times {10}^{4}),$
we conclude that the equation for the velocity is

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}^{2} & =\frac{2\cdot 12\cdot (4\times {10}^{7})^{2}}{r}+(8\times {10}^{4})^{2}-2\cdot 12\cdot (4\times {10}^{7}) \\  & =\frac{384\times {10}^{14}}{r}+(64\times {10}^{8})-(96\times {10}^{7}) \\  & =\frac{3.84\times {10}^{16}}{r}+(6.4\times {10}^{9})-(0.96\times {10}^{9}) \\  & =\frac{3.84\times {10}^{16}}{r}+((6.4-0.96)\times {10}^{9}) \\  & =\frac{3.84\times {10}^{16}}{r}+(5.44\times {10}^{9}).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7
?

Consider a spherical planet with radius (4×107)m and surface gravitational acceleration g=12m/s2. Which equation best models the velocity v of an object projected radially outward from the planet's surface with an initial velocity of (8×104)m/s, where r is the distance from the planet's center to the object. Assume the only force acting on the object is the force due to gravity.

a
v2=3.84×1016r−(5.44×109)
b
v2=3.84×1016r+(5.44×109)
c
v2=3.84×1016r2+(6.4×109)
d
v2=1.92×1016r+(5.44×109)
e
v2=1.92×1016r−(6.4×109)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Let R be the planet's radius and g be the planet's surface gravitational acceleration.

According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, the magnitude of the inward gravitational force pulling the object toward the planet is

Fin=GmMr2,

where G is the gravitational constant, m is the object's mass, and M is the planet's mass.

Since this is the only force and it acts inward, the resultant force, taking outward as positive, is F=−Fin. Applying Newton's second law, F=ma, where a is the acceleration of the object, we have

F=−Finma=−GmMr2a=−GMr2.

In other words, the acceleration is inversely proportional to the square of the distance, a=−kr2, with constant of proportionality k=GM>0.

When at the surface, r=R, the acceleration of the object due to gravity is a=−g. Substituting into our previous equation, we can solve for k:

−g=−kR2⟹k=gR2

Substituting back into the equation, we get

a=−gR2r2.

Now, since acceleration a is the derivative of velocity v, which is the derivative of distance r, we can express acceleration as follows using the chain rule, treating v as a function of r along the trajectory:

a=dvdt=drdt⋅dvdr=vdvdr

Substituting this result into our equation, we obtain a separable differential equation for the velocity:

vdvdr=−gR2r2

Solving using separation of variables, we have

∫vdvdrdr=∫(−gR2r2)dr∫vdv=−gR2∫1r2drv22=−gR2(−1r)+C1v2=2gR2r+C.

Note that C=2C1 is a constant of integration.

Let v0 be the initial velocity of the object. Applying the initial condition v(R)=v0, we can solve for C:

v(R)2=2gR2R+Cv02=2gR+CC=v02−2gR

Therefore, the equation for the velocity of the object is

v2=2gR2r+v02−2gR.

Finally, substituting in the values R=(4×107), g=12, and v0=(8×104), we conclude that the equation for the velocity is v2=2⋅12⋅(4×107)2r+(8×104)2−2⋅12⋅(4×107)=384×1014r+(64×108)−(96×107)=3.84×1016r+(6.4×109)−(0.96×109)=3.84×1016r+((6.4−0.96)×109)=3.84×1016r+(5.44×109).

verification.explanation: The revealed solution declares option b, agreeing with v^2=2gR^2/r+v_0^2-2gR: 2gR^2=3.84×10^16 and v_0^2-2gR=5.44×10^9. The incorrect feedback concerns the deliberately submitted option a.

content.knowledge_point: Solving a Radially Projected Model for Velocity
content.problem: Consider a spherical planet with radius $(4\times {10}^{7})\,\text{m}$ and surface gravitational acceleration $g=12\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$ Which equation best models the velocity $v$ of an object projected radially outward from the planet's surface with an initial velocity of $(8\times {10}^{4})\,\text{m/s},$ where $r$ is the distance from the planet's center to the object. Assume the only force acting on the object is the force due to gravity.
content.worked_solution:
Let $R$ be the planet's radius and $g$ be the planet's surface gravitational acceleration.

According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, the magnitude of the inward gravitational force pulling the object toward the planet is

$$
{F}_{\text{in}}=G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}},
$$

where $G$ is the gravitational constant, $m$ is the object's mass, and $M$ is the planet's mass.

Since this is the only force and it acts inward, the resultant force, taking *outward* as positive, is $F=-{F}_{\text{in}}.$
Applying Newton's second law, $F=ma,$ where $a$ is the acceleration of the object, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =-{F}_{\text{in}} \\ ma & =-G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}} \\ a & =-\frac{GM}{{r}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the acceleration is inversely proportional to the square of the distance,

$$
a=-\frac{k}{{r}^{2}},
$$

with constant of proportionality $k=GM>0.$

When at the surface, $r=R,$ the acceleration of the object due to gravity is $a=-g.$ Substituting into our previous equation, we can solve for $k:$

$$
-g=-\frac{k}{{R}^{2}}\,\,\,⟹\,k=g{R}^{2}
$$

Substituting back into the equation, we get

$$
a=-\frac{g{R}^{2}}{{r}^{2}}.
$$

Now, since acceleration $a$ is the derivative of velocity $v,$ which is the derivative of distance $r,$ we can express acceleration as follows using the chain rule, treating $v$ as a function of $r$ along the trajectory:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{dv}{dt} \\  & =\frac{dr}{dt}\cdot \frac{dv}{dr} \\  & =v\frac{dv}{dr}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this result into our equation, we obtain a separable differential equation for the velocity:

$$
v\frac{dv}{dr}=-\frac{g{R}^{2}}{{r}^{2}}
$$

Solving using separation of variables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int v\frac{dv}{dr}\,dr & =\int (-\frac{g{R}^{2}}{{r}^{2}})\,dr \\ \int v\,dv & =-g{R}^{2}\int \frac{1}{{r}^{2}}\,dr \\ \frac{{v}^{2}}{2} & =-g{R}^{2}(-\frac{1}{r})+{C}_{1} \\ {v}^{2} & =\frac{2g{R}^{2}}{r}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $C=2{C}_{1}$ is a constant of integration.

Let ${v}_{0}$ be the initial velocity of the object. Applying the initial condition $v(R)={v}_{0},$ we can solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(R)^{2} & =\frac{2g{R}^{2}}{R}+C \\ {v}_{0}^{2} & =2gR+C \\ C & ={v}_{0}^{2}-2gR\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation for the velocity of the object is

$$
{v}^{2}=\frac{2g{R}^{2}}{r}+{v}_{0}^{2}-2gR.
$$

Finally, substituting in the values
$R=(4\times {10}^{7}),$
$g=12,$ and
${v}_{0}=(8\times {10}^{4}),$
we conclude that the equation for the velocity is

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}^{2} & =\frac{2\cdot 12\cdot (4\times {10}^{7})^{2}}{r}+(8\times {10}^{4})^{2}-2\cdot 12\cdot (4\times {10}^{7}) \\  & =\frac{384\times {10}^{14}}{r}+(64\times {10}^{8})-(96\times {10}^{7}) \\  & =\frac{3.84\times {10}^{16}}{r}+(6.4\times {10}^{9})-(0.96\times {10}^{9}) \\  & =\frac{3.84\times {10}^{16}}{r}+((6.4-0.96)\times {10}^{9}) \\  & =\frac{3.84\times {10}^{16}}{r}+(5.44\times {10}^{9}).\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 8
?

Consider a spherical planet with radius (1.7×107)m and surface gravitational acceleration g=11.8m/s2. Which equation best models the velocity v of an object projected radially outward from the planet's surface with an initial velocity of (7.4×104)m/s, where r is the distance from the planet's center to the object. Assume the only force acting on the object is the force due to gravity.

a
v2=6.8204×1017r2+(1.464×109)
b
v2=6.8204×1015r+(5.0748×109)
c
v2=8.6204×1015r+(5.0748×109)
d
v2=3.4102×1017r+(1.464×109)
e
v2=6.8204×1015r−(5.0748×109)
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating the gravitational equation gives v^2=2gR^2/r+v_0^2-2gR. Here 2gR^2=6.8204×10^15 and v_0^2-2gR=5.476×10^9-0.4012×10^9=5.0748×10^9, matching option b.

after.name: Question 8
after.problem: Consider a spherical planet with radius $(1.7\times {10}^{7})\,\text{m}$ and surface gravitational acceleration $g=11.8\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$ Which equation best models the velocity $v$ of an object projected radially outward from the planet's surface with an initial velocity of $(7.4\times {10}^{4})\,\text{m/s},$ where $r$ is the distance from the planet's center to the object. Assume the only force acting on the object is the force due to gravity.
after.worked_solution:
Let $R$ be the planet's radius and $g$ be the planet's surface gravitational acceleration.

According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, the magnitude of the inward gravitational force pulling the object toward the planet is

$$
{F}_{\text{in}}=G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}},
$$

where $G$ is the gravitational constant, $m$ is the object's mass, and $M$ is the planet's mass.

Since this is the only force and it acts inward, the resultant force, taking *outward* as positive, is $F=-{F}_{\text{in}}.$
Applying Newton's second law, $F=ma,$ where $a$ is the acceleration of the object, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =-{F}_{\text{in}} \\ ma & =-G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}} \\ a & =-\frac{GM}{{r}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the acceleration is inversely proportional to the square of the distance, 

$$
a=-\frac{k}{{r}^{2}},
$$

with constant of proportionality $k=GM>0.$

When at the surface, $r=R,$ the acceleration of the object due to gravity is $a=-g.$ Substituting into our previous equation, we can solve for $k:$

$$
-g=-\frac{k}{{R}^{2}}\,\,\,⟹\,k=g{R}^{2}
$$

Substituting back into the equation, we get

$$
a=-\frac{g{R}^{2}}{{r}^{2}}.
$$

Now, since acceleration $a$ is the derivative of velocity $v,$ which is the derivative of distance $r,$ we can express acceleration as follows using the chain rule, treating $v$ as a function of $r$ along the trajectory:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{dv}{dt} \\  & =\frac{dr}{dt}\cdot \frac{dv}{dr} \\  & =v\frac{dv}{dr}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this result into our equation, we obtain a separable differential equation for the velocity:

$$
v\frac{dv}{dr}=-\frac{g{R}^{2}}{{r}^{2}}
$$

Solving using separation of variables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int v\frac{dv}{dr}\,dr & =\int (-\frac{g{R}^{2}}{{r}^{2}})\,dr \\ \int v\,dv & =-g{R}^{2}\int \frac{1}{{r}^{2}}\,dr \\ \frac{{v}^{2}}{2} & =-g{R}^{2}(-\frac{1}{r})+{C}_{1} \\ {v}^{2} & =\frac{2g{R}^{2}}{r}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $C=2{C}_{1}$ is a constant of integration.

Let ${v}_{0}$ be the initial velocity of the object. Applying the initial condition $v(R)={v}_{0},$ we can solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(R)^{2} & =\frac{2g{R}^{2}}{R}+C \\ {v}_{0}^{2} & =2gR+C \\ C & ={v}_{0}^{2}-2gR\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation for the velocity of the object is

$$
{v}^{2}=\frac{2g{R}^{2}}{r}+{v}_{0}^{2}-2gR.
$$

Finally, substituting in the values
$R=(1.7\times {10}^{7}),$
$g=11.8,$ and
${v}_{0}=(7.4\times {10}^{4}),$
we conclude that the equation for the velocity is

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}^{2} & =\frac{2\cdot 11.8\cdot (1.7\times {10}^{7})^{2}}{r}+(7.4\times {10}^{4})^{2}-2\cdot 11.8\cdot (1.7\times {10}^{7}) \\  & =\frac{23.6\cdot (2.89\times {10}^{14})}{r}+(54.76\times {10}^{8})-(40.12\times {10}^{7}) \\  & =\frac{68.204\times {10}^{14}}{r}+(54.76\times {10}^{8})-(4.012\times {10}^{8}) \\  & =\frac{6.8204\times {10}^{15}}{r}+((54.76-4.012)\times {10}^{8}) \\  & =\frac{6.8204\times {10}^{15}}{r}+(50.748\times {10}^{8}) \\  & =\frac{6.8204\times {10}^{15}}{r}+(5.0748\times {10}^{9}).\end{aligned}
$$

after.html:
Question 8
?

Consider a spherical planet with radius (1.7×107)m and surface gravitational acceleration g=11.8m/s2. Which equation best models the velocity v of an object projected radially outward from the planet's surface with an initial velocity of (7.4×104)m/s, where r is the distance from the planet's center to the object. Assume the only force acting on the object is the force due to gravity.

a
v2=6.8204×1017r2+(1.464×109)
b
v2=6.8204×1015r+(5.0748×109)
c
v2=8.6204×1015r+(5.0748×109)
d
v2=3.4102×1017r+(1.464×109)
e
v2=6.8204×1015r−(5.0748×109)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let R be the planet's radius and g be the planet's surface gravitational acceleration.

According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, the magnitude of the inward gravitational force pulling the object toward the planet is

Fin=GmMr2,

where G is the gravitational constant, m is the object's mass, and M is the planet's mass.

Since this is the only force and it acts inward, the resultant force, taking outward as positive, is F=−Fin. Applying Newton's second law, F=ma, where a is the acceleration of the object, we have

F=−Finma=−GmMr2a=−GMr2.

In other words, the acceleration is inversely proportional to the square of the distance, a=−kr2, with constant of proportionality k=GM>0.

When at the surface, r=R, the acceleration of the object due to gravity is a=−g. Substituting into our previous equation, we can solve for k:

−g=−kR2⟹k=gR2

Substituting back into the equation, we get

a=−gR2r2.

Now, since acceleration a is the derivative of velocity v, which is the derivative of distance r, we can express acceleration as follows using the chain rule, treating v as a function of r along the trajectory:

a=dvdt=drdt⋅dvdr=vdvdr

Substituting this result into our equation, we obtain a separable differential equation for the velocity:

vdvdr=−gR2r2

Solving using separation of variables, we have

∫vdvdrdr=∫(−gR2r2)dr∫vdv=−gR2∫1r2drv22=−gR2(−1r)+C1v2=2gR2r+C.

Note that C=2C1 is a constant of integration.

Let v0 be the initial velocity of the object. Applying the initial condition v(R)=v0, we can solve for C:

v(R)2=2gR2R+Cv02=2gR+CC=v02−2gR

Therefore, the equation for the velocity of the object is

v2=2gR2r+v02−2gR.

Finally, substituting in the values R=(1.7×107), g=11.8, and v0=(7.4×104), we conclude that the equation for the velocity is

v2=2⋅11.8⋅(1.7×107)2r+(7.4×104)2−2⋅11.8⋅(1.7×107)=23.6⋅(2.89×1014)r+(54.76×108)−(40.12×107)=68.204×1014r+(54.76×108)−(4.012×108)=6.8204×1015r+((54.76−4.012)×108)=6.8204×1015r+(50.748×108)=6.8204×1015r+(5.0748×109).

content.knowledge_point: Solving a Radially Projected Model for Velocity
content.problem: Consider a spherical planet with radius $(1.7\times {10}^{7})\,\text{m}$ and surface gravitational acceleration $g=11.8\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$ Which equation best models the velocity $v$ of an object projected radially outward from the planet's surface with an initial velocity of $(7.4\times {10}^{4})\,\text{m/s},$ where $r$ is the distance from the planet's center to the object. Assume the only force acting on the object is the force due to gravity.
content.worked_solution:
Let $R$ be the planet's radius and $g$ be the planet's surface gravitational acceleration.

According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, the magnitude of the inward gravitational force pulling the object toward the planet is

$$
{F}_{\text{in}}=G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}},
$$

where $G$ is the gravitational constant, $m$ is the object's mass, and $M$ is the planet's mass.

Since this is the only force and it acts inward, the resultant force, taking *outward* as positive, is $F=-{F}_{\text{in}}.$
Applying Newton's second law, $F=ma,$ where $a$ is the acceleration of the object, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =-{F}_{\text{in}} \\ ma & =-G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}} \\ a & =-\frac{GM}{{r}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the acceleration is inversely proportional to the square of the distance, 

$$
a=-\frac{k}{{r}^{2}},
$$

with constant of proportionality $k=GM>0.$

When at the surface, $r=R,$ the acceleration of the object due to gravity is $a=-g.$ Substituting into our previous equation, we can solve for $k:$

$$
-g=-\frac{k}{{R}^{2}}\,\,\,⟹\,k=g{R}^{2}
$$

Substituting back into the equation, we get

$$
a=-\frac{g{R}^{2}}{{r}^{2}}.
$$

Now, since acceleration $a$ is the derivative of velocity $v,$ which is the derivative of distance $r,$ we can express acceleration as follows using the chain rule, treating $v$ as a function of $r$ along the trajectory:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{dv}{dt} \\  & =\frac{dr}{dt}\cdot \frac{dv}{dr} \\  & =v\frac{dv}{dr}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this result into our equation, we obtain a separable differential equation for the velocity:

$$
v\frac{dv}{dr}=-\frac{g{R}^{2}}{{r}^{2}}
$$

Solving using separation of variables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int v\frac{dv}{dr}\,dr & =\int (-\frac{g{R}^{2}}{{r}^{2}})\,dr \\ \int v\,dv & =-g{R}^{2}\int \frac{1}{{r}^{2}}\,dr \\ \frac{{v}^{2}}{2} & =-g{R}^{2}(-\frac{1}{r})+{C}_{1} \\ {v}^{2} & =\frac{2g{R}^{2}}{r}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $C=2{C}_{1}$ is a constant of integration.

Let ${v}_{0}$ be the initial velocity of the object. Applying the initial condition $v(R)={v}_{0},$ we can solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(R)^{2} & =\frac{2g{R}^{2}}{R}+C \\ {v}_{0}^{2} & =2gR+C \\ C & ={v}_{0}^{2}-2gR\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation for the velocity of the object is

$$
{v}^{2}=\frac{2g{R}^{2}}{r}+{v}_{0}^{2}-2gR.
$$

Finally, substituting in the values
$R=(1.7\times {10}^{7}),$
$g=11.8,$ and
${v}_{0}=(7.4\times {10}^{4}),$
we conclude that the equation for the velocity is

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}^{2} & =\frac{2\cdot 11.8\cdot (1.7\times {10}^{7})^{2}}{r}+(7.4\times {10}^{4})^{2}-2\cdot 11.8\cdot (1.7\times {10}^{7}) \\  & =\frac{23.6\cdot (2.89\times {10}^{14})}{r}+(54.76\times {10}^{8})-(40.12\times {10}^{7}) \\  & =\frac{68.204\times {10}^{14}}{r}+(54.76\times {10}^{8})-(4.012\times {10}^{8}) \\  & =\frac{6.8204\times {10}^{15}}{r}+((54.76-4.012)\times {10}^{8}) \\  & =\frac{6.8204\times {10}^{15}}{r}+(50.748\times {10}^{8}) \\  & =\frac{6.8204\times {10}^{15}}{r}+(5.0748\times {10}^{9}).\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 9
?

Consider a spherical planet with radius (2.5×108)m and surface gravitational acceleration g=18.4m/s2. Which equation best models the velocity v of an object projected radially outward from the planet's surface with an initial velocity of (9.6×104)m/s, where r is the distance from the planet's center to the object. Assume the only force acting on the object is the force due to gravity.

a
v2=2.3×1018r−(1.6×107)
b
v2=2.3×1018r2+(9.2×109)
c
v2=1.15×1018r+(1.6×107)
d
v2=1.15×1018r−(9.2×109)
e
v2=2.3×1018r+(1.6×107)
Submit

decision.explanation: The model is v^2=2gR^2/r+v_0^2-2gR. Here 2gR^2=2.3×10^18 and v_0^2-2gR=9.216×10^9-9.2×10^9=1.6×10^7, so option e is correct.

after.name: Question 9
after.problem: Consider a spherical planet with radius $(2.5\times {10}^{8})\,\text{m}$ and surface gravitational acceleration $g=18.4\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$ Which equation best models the velocity $v$ of an object projected radially outward from the planet's surface with an initial velocity of $(9.6\times {10}^{4})\,\text{m/s},$ where $r$ is the distance from the planet's center to the object. Assume the only force acting on the object is the force due to gravity.
after.worked_solution:
Let $R$ be the planet's radius and $g$ be the planet's surface gravitational acceleration.

According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, the magnitude of the inward gravitational force pulling the object toward the planet is

$$
{F}_{\text{in}}=G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}},
$$

where $G$ is the gravitational constant, $m$ is the object's mass, and $M$ is the planet's mass.

Since this is the only force and it acts inward, the resultant force, taking *outward* as positive, is $F=-{F}_{\text{in}}.$
Applying Newton's second law, $F=ma,$ where $a$ is the acceleration of the object, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =-{F}_{\text{in}} \\ ma & =-G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}} \\ a & =-\frac{GM}{{r}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the acceleration is inversely proportional to the square of the distance, 

$$
a=-\frac{k}{{r}^{2}},
$$

 with constant of proportionality $k=GM>0.$

When at the surface, $r=R,$ the acceleration of the object due to gravity is $a=-g.$ Substituting into our previous equation, we can solve for $k:$

$$
-g=-\frac{k}{{R}^{2}}\,\,\,⟹\,k=g{R}^{2}
$$

Substituting back into the equation, we get

$$
a=-\frac{g{R}^{2}}{{r}^{2}}.
$$

Now, since acceleration $a$ is the derivative of velocity $v,$ which is the derivative of distance $r,$ we can express acceleration as follows using the chain rule, treating $v$ as a function of $r$ along the trajectory:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{dv}{dt} \\  & =\frac{dr}{dt}\cdot \frac{dv}{dr} \\  & =v\frac{dv}{dr}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this result into our equation, we obtain a separable differential equation for the velocity:

$$
v\frac{dv}{dr}=-\frac{g{R}^{2}}{{r}^{2}}
$$

Solving using separation of variables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int v\frac{dv}{dr}\,dr & =\int (-\frac{g{R}^{2}}{{r}^{2}})\,dr \\ \int v\,dv & =-g{R}^{2}\int \frac{1}{{r}^{2}}\,dr \\ \frac{{v}^{2}}{2} & =-g{R}^{2}(-\frac{1}{r})+{C}_{1} \\ {v}^{2} & =\frac{2g{R}^{2}}{r}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $C=2{C}_{1}$ is a constant of integration.

Let ${v}_{0}$ be the initial velocity of the object. Applying the initial condition $v(R)={v}_{0},$ we can solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(R)^{2} & =\frac{2g{R}^{2}}{R}+C \\ {v}_{0}^{2} & =2gR+C \\ C & ={v}_{0}^{2}-2gR\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation for the velocity of the object is

$$
{v}^{2}=\frac{2g{R}^{2}}{r}+{v}_{0}^{2}-2gR.
$$

Finally, substituting in the values
$R=(2.5\times {10}^{8}),$
$g=18.4,$ and
${v}_{0}=(9.6\times {10}^{4}),$
we conclude that the equation for the velocity is

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}^{2} & =\frac{2\cdot 18.4\cdot (2.5\times {10}^{8})^{2}}{r}+(9.6\times {10}^{4})^{2}-2\cdot 18.4\cdot (2.5\times {10}^{8}) \\  & =\frac{230\times {10}^{16}}{r}+(92.16\times {10}^{8})-(92\times {10}^{8}) \\  & =\frac{2.3\times {10}^{18}}{r}+((92.16-92)\times {10}^{8}) \\  & =\frac{2.3\times {10}^{18}}{r}+(0.16\times {10}^{8}) \\  & =\frac{2.3\times {10}^{18}}{r}+(1.6\times {10}^{7}).\end{aligned}
$$
